segments.text: This unit surveys major Muslim thinkers who contributed to metaphysics, logic, political philosophy, theology, history, society and reconstruction of religious thought.

Prepare each thinker around two or three central ideas rather than a life story. Al-Farabi: virtuous city and philosophy; Ibn Sina: being/essence and metaphysics; Al-Ghazali: critique of philosophers and spiritual-ethical thought; Ibn Rushd: defense of philosophical reasoning; Ibn Khaldun: society, asabiyyah and historical change; Shah Waliullah: social/religious reform and integrative thought; Iqbal: selfhood, reconstruction and dynamic thought.

blocks.text: Al-Farabi: philosophy, virtue and the political community

segments.text: Al-Farabi develops a philosophical account of human perfection in which knowledge, virtue and political organization are connected. His famous idea of the virtuous city examines how political leadership and social cooperation can orient citizens toward genuine happiness rather than merely wealth, pleasure or domination.

He draws heavily on Plato and Aristotle while working within the intellectual world of classical Islam. His political philosophy is therefore best understood as a synthesis and transformation of Greek philosophical resources, not as a simple copy of Plato’s Republic.

blocks.text: Ibn Sina: metaphysics and the Necessary Existent

segments.text: Ibn Sina builds a systematic philosophy spanning logic, natural philosophy, psychology and metaphysics. A central distinction is between essence—what a thing is—and existence—that it is. Contingent beings do not contain the sufficient explanation of their existence in themselves, leading Ibn Sina’s metaphysics toward the Necessary Existent as the ultimate ground of existence.

His account of the soul, intellect and knowledge became extraordinarily influential in Islamic and Latin philosophy. It should be presented as a coherent system, not reduced to his work as a physician.

blocks.text: Al-Ghazali: critique, theology and the limits of demonstration

segments.text: Al-Ghazali mastered the philosophical tradition he criticized. In The Incoherence of the Philosophers he challenges particular doctrines of the falasifa while accepting and using logic and rigorous argument in other contexts. His work therefore does not support the simplistic claim that he “ended philosophy.”
His broader project joins jurisprudence, theology, ethics and spiritual reform. Philosophically, he is important for debates about causation, certainty, reason and revelation.

blocks.text: Ibn Rushd: demonstration and harmony of philosophy and religion

segments.text: Ibn Rushd was a major jurist and Aristotelian philosopher who defended the legitimate role of demonstrative reasoning in religious inquiry for those qualified to use it. His commentaries helped transmit and reshape Aristotle’s legacy in both Islamic and European traditions.
His disagreement with al-Ghazali should be studied as a precise debate over philosophical doctrines and methods rather than as a crude conflict between “reason” and “religion.”

blocks.text: Ibn Khaldun: society, power and historical explanation

segments.text: Ibn Khaldun’s Muqaddimah develops an analytical approach to social and political change. His concept of asabiyyah concerns group solidarity and capacity for collective action, especially in the rise and consolidation of political power. He also discusses taxation, labour, urban life, education and the reliability of historical reports.
His cyclical observations about dynastic rise and decline are analytical patterns, not an inflexible law that every society must follow in identical stages.

Shah Waliullah sought intellectual and social reform through Qur’anic scholarship, hadith, jurisprudence and an effort to understand the purposes and wisdom of legal and social institutions. His thought is important for connecting normative teaching with social conditions in South Asian Islam.

Muhammad Iqbal’s Reconstruction of Religious Thought in Islam engages modern philosophy, science and Islamic intellectual tradition. Themes include selfhood (khudi), creativity, freedom, time and the reconstruction of religious thought. Iqbal should be read through his arguments, not through isolated inspirational quotations.

items.text: Prepare each thinker through a problem and a few central ideas. Biography matters only when it helps explain the intellectual project.

Al-Farabi links philosophy and political order through the idea of the virtuous city; Ibn Sina develops a sophisticated metaphysics of being and essence; Al-Ghazali critically examines philosophical claims while developing theological and spiritual thought.

Ibn Rushd defends the legitimacy of philosophical reasoning and interprets the relation between philosophy and revelation; Ibn Khaldun explains social cohesion, political rise and decline, and historical method through concepts such as asabiyyah.

Shah Waliullah addresses religious and social reform through an integrative intellectual approach; Iqbal develops selfhood, dynamism and reconstruction of religious thought in engagement with modern philosophy.
Comparative questions should identify both agreement and disagreement. Al-Ghazali versus Ibn Rushd, for example, should not be reduced to “religion versus philosophy.”

rows: Common confusion to avoid: Do not fill answers with quotations you cannot verify. Accurate concepts and references to the thinker's actual works are more valuable.

items.text: Compare Al-Ghazali and Ibn Rushd carefully.
For Iqbal, use his own published works/reliable scholarship for quotations.

segments.text: Muslim philosophy contains internal debate, not one uniform school.
Political, metaphysical and social thought all appear in this unit.
Accurate concepts matter more than decorative quotations.
